prompt: What does the Greek word parousia, used for Christ's expected return, basically mean?
options: Judgment by fire
Presence or arrival, as of a visiting ruler
A thousand-year reign
Resurrection of the dead
correctAnswer: Presence or arrival, as of a visiting ruler
explanation: Parousia means presence or arrival and was used for the visit of a ruler. Early Christians applied it to the return they expected soon.

prompt: An anonymous opponent quoted by Eusebius mocked the Montanists because the end Maximilla foretold had not come more than thirteen years after her death.
explanation: Eusebius preserves this anti-Montanist taunt. The movement survived the failure anyway, for several more centuries.

prompt: How does the Second Letter of Peter answer scoffers who ask where the promise of Christ's coming is?
options: It says the return already happened invisibly in Jerusalem
It sets a new date one generation later
With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and the delay gives time to repent
It says the promise referred only to the apostles' deaths
correctAnswer: With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and the delay gives time to repent
explanation: 2 Peter reframes the delay as divine patience, using the image of a day as a thousand years. Most critical scholars date the letter to the early second century.

prompt: In which Phrygian town, paired with Tymion, did the Montanists expect the heavenly Jerusalem to descend?
explanation: Montanus named Pepuza and Tymion as the site of the New Jerusalem. Around 550 John of Ephesus destroyed the Montanist shrine at Pepuza.

prompt: Contemporary sources show that most of Europe was gripped by a general panic as the year 1000 approached.
explanation: The picture of a continent-wide panic took shape later, above all in nineteenth-century Romantic history. Sources show scattered expectation, not universal terror.

prompt: Which point counts against the legend of a universal panic in the year 1000?
options: No one in the tenth century had heard of Antichrist
Many documents still dated by regnal years, and regions began the year on different days
The Church had banned all talk of the end of the world in 900
Most Europeans used the Islamic calendar
correctAnswer: Many documents still dated by regnal years, and regions began the year on different days
explanation: Anno Domini dating was not yet universal and New Year fell on different days in different regions, so 1000 was not one shared moment. Abbo of Fleury's preacher shows Antichrist talk did exist.

prompt: Match each figure to their role in early or medieval end-time expectation:

pairs.right: Montanist prophet said to have announced that after her would come the end
Latin writer who defended the New Prophecy from about 207 CE
Recalled opposing a Paris preacher who tied Antichrist to the year 1000
Modern historian who argued that expectation around 1000 and 1033 was real

explanation: Each figure marks a stage: an ancient prophet, her defender, a medieval critic of date-setting, and a modern historian reopening the year-1000 debate.

prompt: Find the error in this account of early and medieval expectation:
steps: Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians expects some believers to be alive at Christ's coming
The Gospel of John corrects a rumor that the beloved disciple would not die before Jesus returned
Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla prophesied in Phrygia in the second century
The Montanist movement collapsed within a year of Maximilla's death
Rodulfus Glaber linked portents and famine to the millennium of the Passion in 1033
explanation: Step 4 is wrong. Montanist communities lasted for centuries, until Justinian's measures and the destruction of the Pepuza shrine around 550.

prompt: What did Jan Matthys predict for Easter 1534, and what happened to him?
options: He predicted judgment would fall; he rode out against the besiegers and was killed
He predicted the city's fall; he fled to Leiden
He predicted a famine; he was crowned king
He predicted the bishop's conversion; he died in a Strasbourg prison
correctAnswer: He predicted judgment would fall; he rode out against the besiegers and was killed
explanation: Matthys rode out on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1534, with a small band and was killed. Jan of Leiden then took over the city.

prompt: The iron cages in which the bodies of the executed Münster leaders were displayed still hang from the tower of St Lambert's Church.
explanation: The original cages were taken down in 1881 during the tower's rebuilding and rehung in 1898. They hang there today.

prompt: Which two hostile insiders supply much of what is known about life inside Anabaptist Münster?
options: Menno Simons and Melchior Hoffman
Bernhard Rothmann and Jan Matthys
Heinrich Gresbeck and Hermann von Kerssenbrock
Franz von Waldeck and Bernd Krechting
correctAnswer: Heinrich Gresbeck and Hermann von Kerssenbrock
explanation: Gresbeck was a defector who helped the besiegers in, and Kerssenbrock a Catholic who wrote decades later. Both had reasons to paint the kingdom as monstrous.

prompt: Which Dutch former priest rebuilt the northern Anabaptist movement on nonviolence after Münster, giving his name to a church?
explanation: Menno Simons broke with Rome in 1536 and taught strict nonviolence. The Mennonites take their name from him.

prompt: Polygamy was introduced in Münster in 1534 without any recorded opposition inside the city.
explanation: An armed revolt led by the blacksmith Heinrich Mollenhecke briefly seized Jan of Leiden. After it collapsed, dozens of rebels were executed.

prompt: Who besieged Anabaptist Münster?
options: Emperor Charles V in person
Prince-bishop Franz von Waldeck, later backed by Catholic and Lutheran princes
Bernd Knipperdolling
The city council of Strasbourg
correctAnswer: Prince-bishop Franz von Waldeck, later backed by Catholic and Lutheran princes
explanation: Franz von Waldeck, the city's own prince-bishop, began the siege in 1534. Catholic and Lutheran princes alike later supported him.

prompt: Match each person to their role in the Münster story:

pairs.right: Haarlem baker who claimed to be Enoch and died at Easter 1534
Tailor proclaimed king in September 1534
Cloth merchant who became mayor in February 1534
Preacher who predicted the end for 1533 and died in a Strasbourg prison

explanation: Hoffman inspired the movement, Matthys radicalized it, Knipperdolling gave it civic power and Jan of Leiden turned it into a kingdom.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Münster's end:
steps: Anabaptists won Münster's council elections on 23 February 1534
Jan of Leiden surrendered the city peacefully to the bishop in June 1535
Jan of Leiden, Knipperdolling and Krechting were executed on 22 January 1536
The cages were taken down during the tower's rebuilding and rehung in 1898
In 1987 Lothar Baumgarten placed a light in each cage
explanation: Step 2 is wrong. The city fell on the night of 24 to 25 June 1535 when two defectors, one of them Heinrich Gresbeck, guided the besiegers in, and hundreds of defenders were killed.

prompt: Who proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi the messiah in 1665?
options: Nehemiah ha-Kohen
Gershom Scholem
Nathan of Gaza
Sultan Mehmed IV
explanation: Nathan of Gaza, a young visionary, told Sabbatai he was the messiah in spring 1665 and became the movement's theologian and publicist.

prompt: Sabbatai Zevi converted to Islam in September 1666 after being brought before the court of Sultan Mehmed IV.
explanation: At Edirne, in mid-September 1666, he put on the turban and took the name Aziz Mehmed Efendi.

prompt: How did Nathan of Gaza explain Sabbatai's conversion?
options: The messiah had to descend into the realm of the kelippot to free trapped holy sparks
Sabbatai had been replaced by a double
The conversion was forced and therefore did not count
It proved Sabbatai had never been the messiah
correctAnswer: The messiah had to descend into the realm of the kelippot to free trapped holy sparks
explanation: Nathan drew on Lurianic Kabbalah: ordinary Jews free sparks by keeping the commandments, but the messiah had to enter the husks of evil himself.

prompt: What Turkish name is given to the community of Sabbatai's followers who converted to Islam, centered in Salonica?
explanation: The Dönmeh were outwardly Muslim but kept Sabbatian rites in private. Most moved to Turkey after the population exchange of 1923.

prompt: Gershom Scholem argued that the massacres in Poland and Ukraine of 1648 to 1649 were the main cause of the Sabbatian movement.
explanation: Scholem rejected that older view, noting the movement's strength in Sephardi lands far from Poland. He emphasized the spread of Lurianic Kabbalah instead.

prompt: What does Glückel of Hameln's memoir record about the Sabbatian excitement?
options: She met Sabbatai in Smyrna and wrote his biography
Her father-in-law sent casks of linen and dried food to Hamburg, packed for the journey to the Land of Israel
Her family converted to Islam with him
She led the opposition to him in Amsterdam
correctAnswer: Her father-in-law sent casks of linen and dried food to Hamburg, packed for the journey to the Land of Israel
explanation: The casks stood ready for more than a year. Her memoir shows how far the expectation reached into ordinary households in northern Europe.

prompt: Match each place to its role in Sabbatai Zevi's story:

pairs.right: Port of his birth, where he took over a synagogue in December 1665
Home of the prophet who declared him messiah
Seat of the sultan's court where he converted in 1666
Place of exile where he died in 1676

explanation: The movement's geography runs from an Ottoman port to Gaza, then to the sultan's court and finally to exile on the Adriatic coast.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Sabbatai Zevi:
steps: Sabbatai Zevi was born in Smyrna in 1626
Nathan of Gaza declared him messiah in 1665
He was arrested after sailing for Constantinople in early 1666
He converted to Islam and took the name Aziz Mehmed Efendi
After the conversion, all of his followers abandoned the belief that he was the messiah
explanation: Step 5 is wrong. Nathan gave the conversion a theological meaning, and believers persisted, including the Dönmeh, who imitated Sabbatai's conversion.

prompt: Which verse was central to William Miller's calculation?
options: Revelation 20:4, on the thousand-year reign
Daniel 8:14, on 2,300 days until the sanctuary is cleansed
Genesis 7:4, on seven days before the Flood
Mark 13:30, on 'this generation'
correctAnswer: Daniel 8:14, on 2,300 days until the sanctuary is cleansed
explanation: Miller read the 2,300 days of Daniel 8:14 as 2,300 years and took the cleansing of the sanctuary to mean the purifying of the earth at Christ's return.

prompt: Samuel Snow chose 22 October 1844 because he equated it with the Day of Atonement by Karaite Jewish reckoning.
explanation: Snow's seventh-month message argued that Christ's return would fulfill the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month.

prompt: From what starting year did Miller count the 2,300 years?
options: 586 BCE, the fall of Jerusalem
33 CE, the crucifixion
70 CE, the destruction of the Temple
457 BCE, the decree of Artaxerxes
explanation: Miller dated the decree sending Ezra to Jerusalem to 457 BCE. Adding 2,300 years gave about 1843.

prompt: Which Boston minister and publicist turned Miller's preaching into a national movement?
explanation: Joshua V. Himes organized newspapers, camp meetings, a huge tent and prophetic charts from 1839 onward.

prompt: Reliable contemporary evidence shows that most Millerites waited on rooftops in white ascension robes.
explanation: Investigators from Francis D. Nichol onward found almost no reliable contemporary evidence for the robes. The image came mainly from mockery.

prompt: How did the group that became the Seventh-day Adventists reinterpret 22 October 1844?
options: The calculation was off by exactly one hundred years
Christ had returned secretly to Low Hampton
The date was right, but Christ had entered the Most Holy Place of a heavenly sanctuary
The prophecy referred to the founding of a new state
correctAnswer: The date was right, but Christ had entered the Most Holy Place of a heavenly sanctuary
explanation: Hiram Edson and others kept the date but changed the event. The idea became the doctrine later called the investigative judgment.

prompt: Match each person to their part in the Millerite story:

pairs.right: Farmer and former deist who dated the advent to about 1843
Preacher of the seventh-month message at Exeter, New Hampshire
Wrote that the believers 'wept, and wept, till the day dawn'
Visionary, later Ellen G. White, whose first vision came in December 1844

explanation: Miller supplied the arithmetic, Snow the final date, Edson the reinterpretation, and Ellen White the prophetic guidance of the Seventh-day Adventists.

prompt: Find the error in this account of the Millerites and their heirs:
steps: Miller read each prophetic day in Daniel as a year
He said Christ would come between March 1843 and March 1844
Miller accepted the heavenly sanctuary teaching and helped organize the Seventh-day Adventist Church in 1863
After 22 October 1844 some former Millerites joined the Shakers
The Advent Christian Church was organized in 1860
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. Miller rejected the new sanctuary teaching, kept expecting the advent soon, and died in 1849, fourteen years before the Adventist church was organized.

prompt: According to Dorothy Martin's messages, what would happen before dawn on 21 December 1954?
options: A nuclear war between the superpowers
The return of Jesus to Jerusalem
A solar eclipse that would end the world
A great flood, with believers rescued by flying saucer
correctAnswer: A great flood, with believers rescued by flying saucer
explanation: The messages, said to come from beings on Clarion, warned of a flood and promised rescue of the faithful by saucer.

prompt: Festinger and his colleagues told the Seekers openly that they were social scientists studying the group.
explanation: They used covert participant observation, joining without revealing their purpose and sometimes inventing psychic experiences to gain entry.

prompt: Which is a central methodological criticism of When Prophecy Fails?
options: Covert observers made up a sizable share of the small group and may have reinforced its beliefs
The researchers studied the group only through newspaper clippings
The study relied on a national random survey
The authors first interviewed members twenty years later
correctAnswer: Covert observers made up a sizable share of the small group and may have reinforced its beliefs
explanation: In so small a group the observers' presence was itself an event, and believers read their arrival as a sign. Critics argue this propped up the beliefs being measured.

prompt: What name did Martin's messages give the planet her contacts came from?
explanation: Martin said the messages came from beings on Clarion, above all from Sananda, whom she identified with Jesus.

prompt: Jehovah's Witnesses today teach that 1914 marked Christ's invisible enthronement as king in heaven.
explanation: Russell had expected 1914 to bring the full establishment of God's kingdom on earth. The date was later reinterpreted as an invisible enthronement and the start of the last days.

prompt: What date did the campaign 'Millions Now Living Will Never Die' point to?
options: 1874, the start of Christ's invisible presence
1925, when faithful men of old such as Abraham were expected to return
1975, the end of 6,000 years of human history
1914, the end of the Gentile Times
correctAnswer: 1925, when faithful men of old such as Abraham were expected to return
explanation: Under Rutherford the campaign expected the return of the ancient worthies in 1925. Beth Sarim in San Diego was bought in 1929 to house them.

prompt: Match each person to their role:

pairs.right: Channeled messages from Sananda and later called herself Sister Thedra
Michigan State College physician who lost his post over the beliefs
Lead author of the 1956 study of the group
Reported a 1962 case of a shelter group that did not step up recruiting

explanation: The prophet, her most prominent follower, the lead researcher and a later study that failed to find the predicted surge in proselytizing.

prompt: Find the error in this account of failed prophecy in the twentieth century:
steps: After the 4:45 a.m. message, the Seekers refused all contact with the press
Members in East Lansing who waited mostly alone tended to drift away
The researchers joined the group without revealing their purpose
A 1966 Watch Tower book placed the end of 6,000 years of human history in 1975
In 1995 the Witnesses dropped the teaching that the generation of 1914 would see the end
explanation: Step 1 is wrong. Members who had avoided reporters began calling newspapers within hours and sought publicity in the days that followed.

prompt: What did Harold Camping predict for 21 May 2011?
options: The return of Christ to Jerusalem at noon
The rapture, with a worldwide earthquake at 6 p.m. local time
The physical destruction of the whole world that evening
A nuclear war beginning in the Pacific
correctAnswer: The rapture, with a worldwide earthquake at 6 p.m. local time
explanation: Camping predicted the rapture on 21 May with an earthquake rolling through the time zones, and the destruction of the world on 21 October.

prompt: The Maya Long Count reached the completion of thirteen b'ak'tuns on about 21 December 2012.
explanation: In the most widely used correlation, 13.0.0.0.0 fell on 21 December 2012, with some scholars preferring 23 December. It marked a cycle's completion, not an end.

prompt: What does Tortuguero Monument 6, the only known ancient text that discusses the 2012 date in detail, describe?
options: A flood that will destroy the world in 2012
The arrival of the planet Nibiru
The completion of the thirteenth b'ak'tun and the god Bolon Yokte', with no catastrophe
The end of all Maya calendar counting
correctAnswer: The completion of the thirteenth b'ak'tun and the god Bolon Yokte', with no catastrophe
explanation: The damaged seventh-century inscription mentions the cycle's completion and a god, but no disaster. Other Maya texts project dates thousands of years beyond 2012.

prompt: Which Christian broadcaster, based in Oakland, California, did Harold Camping lead?
explanation: Family Radio carried Camping's predictions worldwide. In 2018 it stopped airing his teaching.

prompt: Research since Festinger shows that a failed prophecy almost always destroys the group that made it.
explanation: Melton and others found that groups usually reinterpret failed dates and survive, especially when they have institutions and purposes beyond the prediction.

prompt: How did Camping respond immediately after 21 May 2011 passed?
options: He blamed infiltrating observers
He said the faithful had saved the world by their light
He said the Maya had chosen the wrong day
He said judgment had come spiritually and moved the physical end to 21 October
correctAnswer: He said judgment had come spiritually and moved the physical end to 21 October
explanation: Spiritualizing the failed date and keeping a second date was a classic move. He acknowledged he had been wrong only in March 2012.

prompt: Match each case to how it turned out:

pairs.right: Dispersed within weeks of the failed date
Lost about two-thirds of members after God failed to appear in Garland, Texas
Grew from a reinterpreted date into a worldwide church
Ended by military conquest, not by disappointment

explanation: Outcomes range from collapse to global growth. What mattered was organization and reinterpretation, and in Münster's case an army.

prompt: Find the error in this account of modern doomsday dates:
steps: J. Gordon Melton argued that believers rarely experience failed prophecy as failure
A common response is to say the event happened spiritually or invisibly
Michael Coe's 1966 suggestion about Armageddon became, and remains, the consensus of Maya specialists
A Palenque inscription projects a date in 4772 CE
Camping acknowledged in March 2012 that he had been wrong
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. Most Maya specialists rejected Coe's Armageddon reading; the only ancient text on the 2012 date describes no catastrophe.
